title: Getting the wrong enquiries? Your website may be attracting the wrong work
description: A practical guide for service businesses whose websites attract the wrong enquiries, with ways to narrow service boundaries, geography, forms, and priority pages.
summary: A website that keeps bringing the wrong enquiries usually has a signal problem, not a traffic problem. Service pages may be too broad, forms may invite almost anyone, or older content may still attract work you no longer want. The fix is to narrow the message, qualify the right visitors, and make the site reflect the jobs you actually want.
takeaways: Wrong enquiries usually come from a mismatch between what the website says and the work you actually want.
Clear service boundaries, geography, and scope signals help the right visitors recognize themselves and help the wrong visitors move on.
Start by auditing declined enquiries and fixing the priority page instead of assuming you need a full redesign.

sections.title: The problem is usually fit, not traffic
sections.body:
Service businesses across the Okanagan often treat every enquiry as a good sign. Then the phone rings with work they do not want, forms arrive from outside the service area, and the calendar starts to fill with the wrong conversations. That is not mainly a visibility problem. It is a fit problem. The website is doing something, but what it is doing is pulling in people whose needs do not match the business.

I see this when a page tries to cover too much ground. It uses broad service language, stays vague about scope, and avoids saying anything that might rule someone out. The result is a site that sounds open to everything. In practice, that usually means it is not especially strong for the work you care about most.

sections.title: Set service boundaries on the page
sections.body:
A good service page should make the boundary obvious. It should say what the business does, who it is for, and what kind of work is a poor fit without sounding defensive. If you only take on projects above a certain size, the page should show that. If you avoid certain job types, the language should be specific enough that people can tell.

A well-made page should also feel considered. Good typography, honest photography, and clear spacing help a visitor trust the business, but they cannot rescue a page that keeps inviting the wrong work. For example, suppose a landscaping company wants design-build projects and does not want to become a small odd-job provider. A page full of broad promises about outdoor work can easily attract the wrong requests. A clearer page would describe the kinds of projects, materials, and outcomes the company actually wants.

sections.title: Let the form do some of the filtering
sections.body:
Forms can help, but they should not become an obstacle. The W3C accessible forms guidance makes a useful point: people generally prefer forms that are simple and ask only for what is needed. That principle works well for lead qualification too. Ask the minimum that helps both sides.

For many service businesses, a few fields are enough. Service type, location, timing, and project size can tell you a lot without turning the form into a long interview. If the form needs to be accessible, keep labels clear, group related fields, and make instructions obvious. If you want a more detailed look at the tradeoff between calls and forms, I have written about calls or forms for a service website.

Sample intake fields for a service business enquiry form
FieldWhat it helps you learn
Service typeWhether the request fits your core work
LocationWhether the person is in your real service area
TimingWhether the request fits your current schedule
Project size or scopeWhether the job clears your minimum scope
Preferred contactWhether follow-up will be simple

sections.title: Make geography and availability obvious
sections.body:
If you work in Kelowna, West Kelowna, Vernon, or Lake Country, say so clearly. Do not make people infer your service area from scattered mentions at the bottom of the page. A local service business should make coverage obvious in the first screen or two. That helps a real person decide quickly, which is more useful than trying to squeeze one more vague phrase into the copy.

The same is true for timing. If you are booking out months ahead, or if you only take certain kinds of work seasonally, make that visible early enough to matter. A visitor who wants urgent help should not need to submit a detailed form to discover that you are not the right fit right now.

sections.title: Match content to the work you want
sections.body:
Wrong enquiries often come from content that no longer reflects the business. Old service pages, broad blog posts, and generic resource pages can all send the wrong signal. A page may still attract traffic, but if it mainly attracts the wrong kind of traffic, it is costing time.

I have seen the value of specificity in local service pages again and again. The useful pages are usually the ones built around real services, real places, and real visitor questions. A page that clearly matches the work you want is generally more helpful than a page that tries to appeal to everyone.

sections.title: Use a wrong-enquiry worksheet
sections.body:
Before rewriting anything, collect a little evidence. Look at the enquiries you declined, the ones that felt too small, too far away, or simply off target. Then compare them against the pages they probably came from. This makes the problem easier to see.

Wrong-enquiry self-audit worksheet
QuestionWhat to look forWhat to change
Which services are producing the wrong enquiries?Requests that do not match your preferred workNarrow the service description and opening copy
Are people asking from outside your service area?Cities or locations that do not fitMake geographic coverage clearer near the top of the page
Are the projects below your minimum scope?Repeated small or odd-job requestsAdd scope signals and be more specific about fit
Is the form too open?Vague or mismatched form submissionsTighten one or two fields without adding friction
Which page seems to be attracting the wrong fit?A pattern tied to one service or articleRewrite that page first instead of changing the whole site

sections.title: Record and review what you turn away
sections.body:
Keep a simple record when you decline an enquiry. Note what was requested, why it was a poor fit, and where it came from if you know. You do not need a complex system for this. A basic note in your inbox, spreadsheet, or CRM is enough if it helps you see a pattern.

Over time, those notes show whether the website needs a better boundary, a clearer area statement, a tighter form, or a different content emphasis. If you need a better way to think about response after the enquiry arrives, see website enquiry follow-up.

sections.title: Change the priority page, not just the words
sections.body:
The best first move is usually to fix the page that is causing the most confusion. Find the service page, article, or contact path that keeps producing the wrong-fit enquiries. Rewrite the opening so the service, audience, scope, and area are obvious. Remove claims that make the page sound broader than the work you actually want.

Sometimes the fix is mostly content. Sometimes it is also structure, forms, or follow-up. If you want the site to reflect the work you want more clearly, that is exactly the kind of web design problem I like to solve. If you are ready to talk through what your own site is attracting and what should change first, get in touch.

faqs: Should I remove a service page if it keeps attracting the wrong work?

Not always. First check whether the page can be narrowed or repositioned. If the work is completely off target and creates more hassle than value, then removal or consolidation may make sense, but often the first step is simply to make the boundary clearer.
Can a very short form attract better enquiries than a longer one?

Often yes, if the short form still asks the right minimum. A shorter form usually lowers friction, which can help good-fit visitors act. The key is to remove unnecessary fields, not to remove all qualification.
What if the wrong enquiries come from search but my service pages look fine?

Then look at the titles, headings, and supporting content around those pages. Search can send people to a page for a phrase that does not match the page's real purpose. A mismatch between search intent and page content can create wrong-fit traffic even when the design is good.
How should I diagnose repeated enquiries for work I do not want?

Record the requested work and the page or campaign that brought the person in when known. Check whether old service descriptions, broad promises or unclear coverage are attracting the wrong audience. Update the relevant pages and form options, then review the quality of subsequent requests rather than aiming to reduce all enquiries.
Should I publish minimum job sizes or service exclusions?

Publish useful boundaries when the business can state them accurately and keep them current. Explain the kind of work you accept and direct customers to the appropriate next step. Avoid discouraging a suitable enquiry with unexplained jargon; clear scope and qualification questions usually help people recognise whether the service fits.
